1086.title: The Friday sermon
1086.hook: two sermons before the Friday prayer, listened to in silence
1086.howItsDone: Each Friday at midday, Muslims gather at the mosque for jumu'ah: the imam gives two sermons with a short sit between them, the congregation listens in silence, and then they pray together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jama'ah: prayer in rows, together. Today the row sits down and listens.

Medina, a Friday. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is standing and speaking to the people. Then a noise from the edge of town: a trade caravan has arrived, with goods to buy and the clamor of a market day. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says people got up and went, and only a few stayed seated. The Qur'an kept the moment. In Pickthall's translation: "But when they spy some merchandise or pastime they break away to it and leave thee standing." The caravans are smaller now. They fit in a pocket, and they buzz.
screen: `A FRIDAY IN MEDINA.` → `THE CARAVAN ARRIVES.` → `THEY LEAVE HIM STANDING.`

segments.voice: Khutbah means a sermon, an address. On Friday, the congregational prayer called jumu'ah is preceded by one; you met it in year two, with leave trade for a while. First, its shape. Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet gave two sermons on Friday and sat briefly between them. So the imam stands, speaks, sits a moment, stands again, speaks again, and only then the prayer begins. Second, the call. Eight days ago this path heard surah sixty-two's command to haste unto remembrance of Allah when the call is heard. In Pickthall's translation the verse goes on: "and leave your trading." The same surah that keeps the caravan story tells people, two verses earlier, to put the market down when the call comes. Third, the silence. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that if you tell the person beside you to be quiet while the imam is speaking, you yourself have spoken idly. Even the shush counts. You listen, and let the person beside you do their own listening. Fourth, what the silence is for. The congregation hears a person speak to them about this week, this city, these lives. Some of it lands, some doesn't. The command is the same either way: the market waits, the shush waits, the phone waits. The caravan story ends with a line that answers it, in Pickthall's words: "That which Allah hath is better than pastime and than merchandise."
screen: `TWO SERMONS, A SIT BETWEEN.` · `LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `EVEN THE SHUSH COUNTS.` · `THE MARKET WAITS.` · then, large: `BETTER THAN PASTIME AND THAN MERCHANDISE.`

segments.voice: Put your phone out of reach, or face-down and silent if this lesson is playing on it, and listen to the room: the hum of something electric, a car outside, your own breath, without naming or judging any of it. If you attend the Friday prayer, you can leave the phone off or in the car this week and give the khutbah your whole hearing. If you don't, give one person a conversation with no screen anywhere in it.
Khutbah. The sermon: on Friday, two addresses before the prayer, heard in a silence so full it leaves no room even for shushing. Today's word.
Your line: silence for the khutbah. The market, the shush and the phone can all wait. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1087.title: Praying while traveling
1087.hook: travelers shorten four-unit prayers to two, and may combine some
1087.howItsDone: Muslims on a journey pray the noon, afternoon and night prayers as two units each, and depending on their school may combine noon with afternoon and sunset with night; schools set their own rules on distance and length of stay.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the khutbah: two sermons on Friday, heard in full silence. Today we leave the mosque and hit the road.

A highway rest stop, the engine ticking as it cools. A family has been on the road since breakfast, and the noon prayer has come in. The kids stretch their legs by a picnic table. Their father spreads a thin mat on the grass beside the car, faces the direction his phone gives him, prays, and is done sooner than at home. Shorter than usual, by design. Islam has a rule for the road, and it starts with a verse and a question someone once put to Umar.
screen: `A REST STOP, ENGINE COOLING.` → `A MAT ON THE GRASS.` → `SHORTER, BY DESIGN.`

segments.voice: Qasr means shortening. On a journey, the four-unit prayers, noon, afternoon and night, are prayed as two. Dawn and sunset stay as they are. First, the verse. Pickthall's translation of surah four says that when ye go forth in the land, "it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship," then adds a condition: if you fear an attack. Second, the question. A man named Ya'la asked Umar ibn al-Khattab: people are safe now, so why do we still shorten? Umar said he had wondered the same, and had asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who answered: it is a charity God has given you, so accept His charity. That's in Sahih Muslim. Four days ago, two units of duha were a charity paid for your joints. Here it runs the other way: God gives it, and the traveler's job is to take it. Third, an old memory. Aisha said, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the prayer was first prescribed as two units, then the traveler's prayer was kept that way while the prayer at home was lengthened. On that report, the shortened prayer is the older shape. Fourth, combining. On journeys the Prophet sometimes joined the noon and afternoon prayers, or sunset and night. Here the schools part ways. The Hanafi school holds shortening required for a traveler, and allows combining only during the hajj, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Other schools treat shortening as a permission and allow combining on journeys. They also differ on how far counts as a journey, and how long a stay ends it. Each reads the same reports with care.
screen: `FOUR BECOME TWO.` · `NO SIN TO CURTAIL.` · `A CHARITY: ACCEPT IT.` · `THE SCHOOLS PART WAYS.` · then, large: `ACCEPT HIS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Notice what you're carrying in your body, raised shoulders, a tight jaw, a gripping hand, and let one thing go with each breath; then bring your next trip to mind. If you pray, you might find out from a teacher or a trusted book of your school how far counts as a journey and whether you may combine. If you don't, notice one load you could set down on that trip.
Qasr. Shortening: on a journey, the four-unit prayers are prayed as two, a charity from God to accept. Today's word.
Your line: lighter on the road. A charity from God, there to be accepted. See you tomorrow.

1088.title: Forgetting in prayer
1088.hook: two prostrations at the end if you forget
1088.howItsDone: When Muslims add to, leave out, or lose count in a prayer, they make two extra prostrations near its end, before or after the closing salam depending on their school, and the prayer stands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qasr: the four-unit prayers shortened to two on the road. Today, a prayer that comes out short by accident.

An afternoon prayer in Medina. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ leads it, and ends it after two units. A four-unit prayer, finished at two. He goes and leans against a piece of wood in the mosque. People stand around, uneasy. Then a man the companions nicknamed Dhul-Yadayn, the one with the long hands, asks: has the prayer been shortened, or did you forget? Neither, as far as he knows, he answers, and he turns to the others. Is it true? It's true. So he goes back, prays what he left out, and adds today's word at the end.
screen: `FOUR UNITS, ENDED AT TWO.` → `THE MAN WITH THE LONG HANDS.` → `SHORTENED, OR FORGOTTEN?`

segments.voice: Sujud al-sahw means the prostrations of forgetfulness: two extra prostrations near the end of the prayer, made when something was added, left out, or is in doubt. First, that story, from Sahih al-Bukhari. Nobody was shamed. The prayer wasn't thrown out. The missing units were prayed, and two prostrations mended it. Second, what the Prophet said about himself. Another report in Bukhari has him say, after a slip in prayer: I am only a human being like you. I forget as you forget. So when I forget, remind me. That line comes from the one who had just led the prayer. Third, doubt. A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives a familiar case: you can't remember whether you've prayed three units or four. Throw the doubt away, it says, and build on what you're sure of, then make two prostrations before you finish. Not start over. Not stand there replaying it. Fourth, where the schools differ: whether the two prostrations come before the closing salam or after it. The Hanafi school places them after. The Shafi'i school places them before. The Maliki school depends on whether something was added or left out, and the Hanbali school follows the specific report for each case. They agree on the main thing: the prayer comes with its own repair kit.
screen: `ENDED EARLY, THEN MENDED.` · `I FORGET AS YOU FORGET.` · `BUILD ON WHAT YOU'RE SURE OF.` · `BEFORE THE SALAM, OR AFTER?` · then, large: `WHEN I FORGET, REMIND ME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small mistake from this week, a forgotten call, a missed step, a word in the wrong place, and see it without replaying it; then picture one small step that would mend it, and let the replaying go on the out-breath. If you pray, remember the two prostrations next time you lose count, and mend the prayer rather than abandon it. If you don't, simply set the mistake down, and leave it there.
Sujud al-sahw. The prostrations of forgetfulness: two prostrations near the end of the prayer that mend a slip. Today's word.
Your line: mistakes are expected. Even the Prophet said: I forget as you forget. Same time tomorrow.

1089.title: The prostration of thanks
1089.hook: a single prostration at good news (Abu Dawud)
1089.howItsDone: On hearing good news or being spared a harm, Muslims who keep this practice make a single prostration of thanks, outside the regular prayer; schools differ on whether wudu and facing the qibla are needed for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sujud al-sahw: two prostrations that mend a slip. Today, a prostration for the opposite of a mistake.

Ka'b ibn Malik has been waiting a long time. He stayed home from a military expedition with no excuse, and when the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ returned, Ka'b told the plain truth instead of inventing one. Since then, by his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari, people have stopped speaking to him. Then one morning, after the dawn prayer, on the roof of his house, he hears a voice shouting from a hill: Ka'b ibn Malik, good news! Before he stands, before he runs to anyone, before he says a word, his body answers. He falls down in prostration.
screen: `HE TOLD THE PLAIN TRUTH.` → `A VOICE FROM THE HILL.` → `HE FALLS DOWN IN PROSTRATION.`

segments.voice: Sujud al-shukr means the prostration of thanks: a single prostration, on its own, outside the regular prayer, made when good news arrives or a harm is lifted. First, the Prophet's habit. Abu Dawud records that when something delighted him, or he was given good news, he would fall down in prostration, giving thanks to God. No bowing first, no units, no closing salam. Just down. Second, why the body. In the five prayers the prostration is the lowest point, forehead on the floor. Using that posture for joy says the place of greatest humility is also the place of thanks. Third, the promise behind it. Pickthall's translation of surah fourteen has God say: "If ye give thanks, I will give you more." Thanks, in that verse, isn't just good manners. It opens a door. Fourth, the details, where scholars differ. Some hold that because it's a prostration, it needs wudu and facing the qibla, like prayer. Others say it isn't a prayer at all, so good news can be answered on the spot. Within the Maliki school a well-known view did not encourage it, while others in the same school accepted it. Go back to Ka'b on his roof. The report doesn't have him checking his wudu or which way he faced. It just says he fell down. Whatever a school decides about the details, the first move is the same. Good news comes, and the forehead goes to the ground.
screen: `DOWN AT GOOD NEWS.` · `THE LOWEST PLACE, FOR JOY.` · `IF YE GIVE THANKS.` · `WUDU, OR ON THE SPOT?` · then, large: `IF YE GIVE THANKS, I WILL GIVE YOU MORE.`

segments.voice: Let one piece of good news from the last while come back in full: a test result, a message, a child's laugh, a debt paid off, a pain that eased. If you pray, you can make a single prostration of thanks now, or keep the habit ready for the next good news. If you don't, bow your head or rest your palms flat on the floor, and let the body say thanks before the mouth does.
Sujud al-shukr. The prostration of thanks: one prostration, on its own, when good news comes. Today's word.
Your line: down, in thanks. The lowest place is also the place of joy. Until tomorrow.

1090.title: The eclipse and the rain
1090.hook: special prayers for an eclipse and for rain
1090.howItsDone: When there is a solar or lunar eclipse, Muslims gather at mosques for the eclipse prayer, with long recitation, until it passes; in times of drought, communities go out to an open prayer ground for the rain prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sujud al-shukr: one prostration of thanks when good news comes. Today, prayers for when the sky itself changes.

The sun went dark over Medina on the day Ibrahim died. He was the son of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says people began to say it: the sun has eclipsed because Ibrahim died. It would have been easy to let them. It was a kind thing to say, and it honored a grieving father. Instead, on the day of his own loss, the Prophet stood up and corrected them.
screen: `THE SUN GOES DARK.` → `BECAUSE IBRAHIM DIED?` → `HE CORRECTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Islam keeps special prayers for two changes in the sky: the eclipse and the drought. First, what he said. The sun and the moon are two of the signs of God. They do not eclipse for anyone's death or for anyone's life. When you see it, pray, and call on God, until it clears. He turned a rumor that flattered him into a prayer pointed away from himself. Second, the eclipse prayer, salat al-kusuf. Aisha's report in Bukhari describes it prayed in congregation, with very long standing and recitation, and an extra bowing in each unit. Here the schools differ: the Hanafi school prays it in the form of ordinary units; the other schools follow the reports with the extra bowing. Both pray until the light returns. Third, the rain. Salat al-istisqa is the prayer asking for rain. Another report in Bukhari says the Prophet went out to the open prayer ground, faced the qibla, turned his cloak around, and prayed two units. Some scholars read the turned cloak as a hope that the season would turn too. Fourth, a Friday story, picking up from the khutbah four days ago. During the sermon, a man stood and said the animals were dying and the roads were cut: ask God for rain. The Prophet raised his hands and asked. The report says rain fell, and kept falling until the next Friday, when a man stood and asked for it to stop. So the Prophet asked again, for rain around them and not upon them. Too dark, too dry, too wet: each one met with a prayer.
screen: `NOT FOR ANYONE'S DEATH.` · `PRAY UNTIL IT CLEARS.` · `THE CLOAK TURNED AROUND.` · `AROUND US, NOT UPON US.` · then, large: `EVERY SKY HAS ITS PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Look out a window, or remember the last sky you saw, and stay with its color, its light, the clouds or the lack of them, for a few breaths. If you pray, you might ask a teacher of your school how the eclipse and rain prayers are prayed, and when your mosque holds them. If you don't, let the next change in the weather stop you for one full breath.
The eclipse and the rain. Two special prayers, salat al-kusuf when the sun or moon darkens, salat al-istisqa when rain is needed. Today's word.

1091.title: Presence in prayer
1091.hook: a heart that knows what it says
1091.howItsDone: Muslims seeking khushu' learn the meanings of what they recite, pray slowly, keep their gaze on the place of prostration, and clear distractions from the place where they pray.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the eclipse and the rain: a prayer for every kind of sky. Today, what happens inside any prayer.

A cloak with markings woven into it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ prays in it, and during the prayer his eye catches the markings. Afterward, a report in Sahih al-Bukhari says, he hands it back: take this to Abu Jahm, and bring me his plain one instead, because this distracted me in my prayer. A garment, given away for being too interesting. It's a small story, and it fits anyone who has finished a prayer, or a song, or a sentence, and not heard a word of it.
screen: `A CLOAK WITH MARKINGS.` → `IT CAUGHT HIS EYE.` → `BRING ME THE PLAIN ONE.`

segments.voice: Khushu' is presence in prayer: a stillness of body and a heart that is there, humble, attending. You met it in year two; today, a closer look. First, the Qur'an puts it at the head of a list. Surah twenty-three opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Successful indeed are the believers Who are humble in their prayers." The Arabic word behind humble shares a root with today's word. Success begins with how a person stands in prayer. Second, the line in today's carry. Surah four tells believers not to draw near to prayer while drunk, and Pickthall gives the reason: "till ye know that which ye utter." The verse is about intoxication, but some readers hear in its last words what prayer is for: knowing what you're saying while you say it. Third, why the words matter. A hadith in Sahih Muslim, in which the Prophet relates God's words, says the prayer is divided between God and the one praying, and each line of al-Fatiha gets an answer. The person says, in Pickthall's words, "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds," and God says: My servant has praised Me. "The Beneficent, the Merciful," and God says: My servant has extolled Me. Line after line. On that hadith, al-Fatiha isn't only a recitation. It's a conversation, and one side is answering. Fourth, the cloak again. Even the Prophet removed a distraction rather than fighting it. So khushu' can start with the room: a plain wall, a quiet corner, the phone somewhere else. Make it easier to be there, then be there.

1092.title: The prayer as rest
1092.hook: the Prophet ﷺ said: give us rest by it, Bilal (Abu Dawud)
1092.howItsDone: Muslims pray the daily prayers, and teachers sometimes recall the Prophet's words to Bilal, 'give us rest by it,' to encourage praying unhurried, as a relief rather than a chore.

segments.voice: Yesterday, khushu': presence in prayer, knowing what you say. Today, the last day on the prayer.

A man sitting with a few people says out loud that he wishes he had prayed, so he could have found some rest. The others seem to find that odd, and they let him know. Rest? Prayer is a duty. You get it done. So he answers with something he heard the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ say. The report is in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. The Prophet would turn to Bilal, the man who called the prayer, and say: Bilal, call the iqamah, and give us rest by it. Not rest after it. Rest by it.
screen: `I WISH I HAD PRAYED, AND RESTED.` → `REST? IT'S A DUTY.` → `BILAL, GIVE US REST BY IT.`

segments.voice: First, the Arabic the report gives: arihna biha. Give us rest by it, or with it. Some teachers point at that small word, biha, by it. There's a way of praying that sounds like the opposite: give us rest from it, let's get this over with. The words in the report go the other way. The prayer isn't the task standing between you and your rest. It is the rest. Second, the Qur'an puts it plainly in surah thirteen, in Pickthall's words: "Verily in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest!" The prayer is remembrance in a body: standing, bowing, putting the forehead on the ground. Another report, in the Sunan of an-Nasa'i, has the Prophet ﷺ say that the comfort of his eye was placed in the prayer. Comfort of the eye is an Arabic way of saying the thing you're glad to look at, the thing that settles you. Third, look back at this week. The Friday sermon, heard in silence. The lighter prayer on the road. Two prostrations when you forget, because mistakes are expected. One prostration of thanks at good news. A prayer for every kind of sky. And yesterday, knowing what you say. Each of those makes the prayer a little less like a test you pass and more like a room you walk into. Fourth, an ordinary day. Several times a day the world stops asking you for things for a few minutes. The inbox can wait. For Muslims, that pause is required, and the report says it was meant to feel like relief, not like one more thing on the list.
screen: `ARIHNA BIHA: GIVE US REST BY IT.` · `IN REMEMBRANCE, HEARTS FIND REST.` · `THIS WEEK, BUILDING TO REST.` · `A ROOM YOU WALK INTO.` · then, large: `VERILY IN THE REMEMBRANCE OF ALLAH DO HEARTS FIND REST!`

segments.voice: If you pray, take your next prayer slowly, and in each position, standing, bowing, prostrating, let one thing you're carrying go down with you. If you don't, breathe in and notice what you're holding, a task, a worry, a conversation, then breathe out and set it on the floor beside you. You don't have to finish anything.
The prayer as rest. Arihna biha: give us rest by it. The Prophet's words to Bilal, and the close of the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: rest in it. Tomorrow, a new pillar, and a word that means two things at once. Rest well.
